question: Mangal Pandey, whose act at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 is called the first major incident of the Sepoy Mutiny, was a sepoy of which regiment?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 34th Bengal Native Infantry.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mangal Pandey belonged to the 34th Bengal Native Infantry stationed at Barrackpore near Calcutta, and he refused to bite the new greased cartridges of the Enfield rifle (34वीं बंगाल नेटिव इन्फैंट्री का सिपाही मंगल पांडे)

 

• On 29 March 1857 he attacked Lt. Baugh and wounded Sergeant-Major Hewson on the parade ground, though no British officer was actually killed.

 

• He was tried and hanged at Barrackpore on 8 April 1857, and his regiment was disbanded as a punishment for failing to restrain him.

 

• His act is treated as the spark that made the sepoys' discontent visible, preceding the general outbreak at Meerut by about six weeks.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mangal Pandey was a Brahmin sepoy from the Ballia region of Uttar Pradesh according to most accounts.

 

• The Enfield rifle's cartridge had to be bitten open before loading, which offended both Hindu and Muslim soldiers.

 

• The Barrackpore incident is dated 29 March 1857, whereas the general rising at Meerut came on 10 May 1857.

 

NOTE

 

• 19th Bengal Native Infantry (Option 2): The 19th Native Infantry was posted at Berhampur in Bengal and was the unit that refused the cartridges there in February 1857, well before Mangal Pandey acted; it was not his regiment.

 

• 3rd Bengal Light Cavalry (Option 3): The 3rd Cavalry was at Meerut, where eighty-five troopers who refused the cartridges were jailed in May 1857, an episode quite separate from the Barrackpore incident involving Mangal Pandey.

 

• 11th Bengal Native Infantry (Option 4): The 11th Native Infantry is a distractor with no link to Mangal Pandey; he served with the 34th at Barrackpore, which is why that regiment was disbanded after his execution.

question: On which date was Mangal Pandey hanged at Barrackpore for attacking his British officers?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 8 April 1857.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mangal Pandey was executed by hanging on 8 April 1857 at Barrackpore, about ten days after his attack on the officers of his regiment (मंगल पांडे को 8 अप्रैल 1857 को फाँसी दी गई)

 

• His attack took place on 29 March 1857; he wounded Lt. Baugh and Sergeant-Major Hewson, and a jamadar, Ishwari Prasad, was also hanged for not helping to arrest him.

 

• The regiment he belonged to, the 34th Bengal Native Infantry, was disbanded and other guilty sepoys were punished.

 

• Because the execution came so early, it is regarded as a prelude to the Meerut outbreak and not as the formal beginning of the Revolt.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The formal outbreak of the Revolt of 1857 is dated 10 May 1857 at Meerut, a different date from the execution.

 

• Mangal Pandey's name later became a symbol of resistance, and the term 'Pandy' was used by the British for rebel sepoys.

 

• India Post issued a commemorative stamp on Mangal Pandey in 1984.

 

NOTE

 

• 29 March 1857 (Option 1): 29 March 1857 is the date of Mangal Pandey's attack on Lt. Baugh and Sergeant-Major Hewson, not of his hanging, which followed after a trial and fell in the first week or so of April.

 

• 10 May 1857 (Option 2): 10 May 1857 marks the sepoys' rising at Meerut, when troopers shot their officers and marched to Delhi; Mangal Pandey had already been executed more than a month earlier.

 

• 12 June 1857 (Option 3): 12 June 1857 is unrelated to Mangal Pandey; by that date the Revolt had spread widely, and he had been hanged at Barrackpore in the first half of April.

question: The immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857 was the introduction of cartridges for which rifle, rumoured to be greased with beef and pig fat?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Enfield rifle (P-53).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Enfield Rifle (Pattern 1853) was newly introduced in the Company's army, and its cartridge had to be bitten open before loading, which turned a military matter into a religious grievance (नई एनफील्ड राइफल के कारतूस पर गाय और सूअर की चर्बी की अफवाह)

 

• The grease was believed to be a mixture of beef and pig fat, which wounded the feelings of Hindu sepoys (cow is sacred) and Muslim sepoys (pig is unclean).

 

• The sepoys concluded that the government was deliberately trying to destroy their religious and cultural identity.

 

• Though the Company later allowed sepoys to grease the cartridges themselves, trust had already collapsed and the 19th Native Infantry at Berhampur became the first to refuse.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Brown Bess was the older smooth-bore flintlock musket, which the Enfield rifle was replacing in the Company's Bengal Army.

 

• The Revolt is also called the Sepoy Mutiny because it started within the Company's Bengal Army.

 

• Lord Canning was Governor-General when the Enfield rifle controversy broke out.

 

NOTE

 

• Brown Bess musket (Option 1): The Brown Bess was an older smooth-bore flintlock musket used by the Company's troops for decades before 1857; it was the weapon the Enfield replaced, and the grease rumour attached only to the new Enfield cartridges.

 

• Martini-Henry rifle (Option 3): The Martini-Henry rifle came into British service only in the 1870s, long after the Revolt, so it cannot have been the weapon whose cartridges triggered the sepoys' protest.

 

• Lee-Metford rifle (Option 4): The Lee-Metford rifle was adopted in the late 1880s and 1890s, decades after 1857, and has no connection with the greased-cartridge episode that began the sepoy unrest.

question: Which regiment at Berhampur refused to use the Enfield cartridges and raised the banner of revolt before the Barrackpore incident?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 19th Native Infantry.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The 19th Native Infantry stationed at Berhampur (Bengal) refused the new cartridges in February 1857, and it was disarmed and disbanded (बहरामपुर की 19वीं नेटिव इन्फैंट्री ने कारतूस लेने से इनकार किया)

 

• This was the earliest open refusal, which showed that unrest over the greased cartridges had begun in Bengal even before Mangal Pandey's attack of 29 March 1857.

 

• Its refusal belongs to the sequence of Berhampur (February), Barrackpore (29 March) and Meerut (April-May), which led up to the general rising.

 

• The incident convinced the soldiers that the authorities were set on defiling their faith, and it fed rumours that spread to other cantonments.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Berhampur is located in Murshidabad district of West Bengal.

 

• The Bengal Army, which contained many high-caste Brahmin and Rajput sepoys from Awadh and Bihar, was the main site of the revolt.

 

• The 34th Native Infantry was disbanded after Mangal Pandey's act, which is a separate episode.

 

• After Berhampur the sepoy discontent spread to Barrackpore in March and Meerut in May 1857, and offers to let soldiers grease their own cartridges came too late to restore trust.

 

NOTE

 

• 34th Native Infantry (Option 1): The 34th Native Infantry was at Barrackpore and became known for Mangal Pandey's attack on 29 March 1857, which came after the Berhampur refusal rather than being the first protest.

 

• 7th Awadh Irregular Infantry (Option 2): The 7th Awadh Irregular Infantry did mutiny at Lucknow in 1857, but this was a different regiment and a later episode than the Berhampur refusal at the outset.

 

• 3rd Light Cavalry (Option 3): The 3rd Light Cavalry was posted at Meerut, where eighty-five troopers refused the cartridges in May 1857; that incident came months after Berhampur and triggered the open outbreak.

question: The Revolt of 1857 formally began on 10 May 1857 at:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Meerut.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sepoys at Meerut broke into open rebellion on 10 May 1857, shot their officers and released their imprisoned comrades (10 मई 1857 को मेरठ से विद्रोह की औपचारिक शुरुआत)

 

• The trigger was the sentencing of eighty-five troopers of the 3rd Cavalry to long imprisonment for refusing the greased cartridges.

 

• The rebels set off for Delhi shouting 'March to Delhi' ('Delhi Chalo'), reaching the Mughal capital and winning over its garrison.

 

• Meerut is therefore counted as the starting point of the Revolt, while Gwalior is treated as the place where it effectively ended in June 1858.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Meerut is in present-day Uttar Pradesh and was a large cantonment with European and Indian troops.

 

• Delhi was reached on the following day, and on 12 May the elderly Bahadur Shah II was proclaimed Shahenshah-e-Hindustan.

 

• The slogan 'Delhi Chalo' was later revived by Subhas Chandra Bose for the INA.

 

NOTE

 

• Barrackpore (Option 1): Barrackpore saw Mangal Pandey's attack on 29 March 1857; it was a precursor and a single-man act rather than the formal outbreak in which sepoys rose in a body.

 

• Kanpur (Option 3): Kanpur joined the rising in June 1857 under Nana Sahib after the Meerut and Delhi events, so it was a later centre of the Revolt, not its starting point.

 

• Lucknow (Option 4): Lucknow rose in 1857 under Begum Hazrat Mahal after Awadh's annexation, but this was weeks after Meerut; it was not where the first rebellion of the sepoys took place.

question: Eighty-five sepoys sentenced to long imprisonment for refusing the cartridges in the events leading to the Meerut outbreak belonged to which unit?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 3rd Cavalry.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The eighty-five men were troopers of the 3rd Cavalry at Meerut, who refused to accept the greased cartridges when ordered to parade (मेरठ में 3rd कैवेलरी के 85 सैनिकों को लंबी कैद)

 

• They were publicly stripped of their uniforms, shackled and jailed in early May 1857, which humiliated the whole garrison.

 

• On 10 May 1857 their comrades broke open the jail, killed British officers and set out for Delhi, so the sentence is the immediate prelude to the formal outbreak.

 

• This explains why Meerut, and not Barrackpore or Berhampur, is accepted as the starting centre of the great Revolt.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The sentence was passed by a court-martial, and the event happened on the eve of the rising.

 

• Meerut also housed Rifles and artillery units, but the first spark came from the cavalry and infantry sepoys together.

 

• Bahadur Shah II was proclaimed emperor at Delhi on 12 May 1857, two days after the Meerut rising.

 

NOTE

 

• 34th Native Infantry (Option 2): The 34th Native Infantry was the regiment of Mangal Pandey at Barrackpore, hundreds of kilometres from Meerut, and its trouble arose in March, not in the cavalry episode of May.

 

• 19th Native Infantry (Option 3): The 19th Native Infantry was at Berhampur and had refused the cartridges in February 1857; it was not involved in the Meerut jail sentence of eighty-five troopers.

 

• Gurkha Rifles (Option 4): Gurkha units remained largely loyal to the Company during the Revolt and helped to recapture Delhi, so they were not among the men sentenced for refusing the cartridges.

question: After capturing Delhi, the rebels proclaimed which ruler as 'Shahenshah-e-Hindustan' (Emperor of India)?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bahadur Shah II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• On 12 May 1857 the rebels at Delhi proclaimed the aged, nominal Mughal king Bahadur Shah II (Zafar) as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan (बहादुर शाह द्वितीय को हिंदुस्तान का शहंशाह घोषित किया गया)

 

• This gave the rising a legitimising symbol, because the Mughal court still carried emotional authority across northern India.

 

• Real control in Delhi, however, was exercised by his army general Bakht Khan, since the emperor was elderly and had little military role.

 

• After Delhi's fall he was deported to Rangoon in 1858 and died there in 1862.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bahadur Shah II wrote Urdu poetry under the pen name Zafar and was the last Mughal emperor.

 

• He was captured by Captain Hodson at Humayun's Tomb in September 1857 after Delhi was retaken.

 

• His sons were shot dead by Hodson near Khooni Darwaza.

 

• Bahadur Shah II ruled from 1837, succeeding Akbar II, and the Company had already signalled that the Mughal royal title would end with his death, which added to the court's resentment.

 

NOTE

 

• Wajid Ali Shah (Option 1): Wajid Ali Shah was the Nawab of Awadh, removed from his throne when Awadh was annexed in 1856 and sent to Calcutta; he was not proclaimed emperor at Delhi in May 1857.

 

• Nana Sahib (Option 3): Nana Sahib was the adopted son of the last Peshwa Baji Rao II and led the rising at Kanpur; he never took a Mughal imperial title or held the throne of Delhi.

 

• Shah Alam II (Option 4): Shah Alam II died in 1806, over fifty years before the Revolt, so he could not have been proclaimed emperor by the 1857 rebels at Delhi.

question: Who exercised real military control at Delhi during the Revolt of 1857 as the army general of Bahadur Shah Zafar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bakht Khan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bakht Khan, a former artillery subedar who came from Bareilly with his troops, became the effective commander of the rebel army in Delhi (दिल्ली में बख्त खान ने वास्तविक सैन्य नेतृत्व किया)

 

• Bahadur Shah Zafar was the symbolic head, and was too old and politically weak to command, so authority rested with Bakht Khan.

 

• The Delhi centre fell on 20 September 1857 when British forces under John Nicholson stormed the city after a prolonged siege.

 

• Bakht Khan later retreated to Awadh and continued the fight in the region around Lucknow.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Delhi court also saw friction between the emperor's sons and the rebel commanders over finances and control.

 

• John Nicholson was fatally wounded during the assault on Delhi and died soon after.

 

• Captain Hodson's capture of Bahadur Shah ended the Delhi leadership.

 

• Bakht Khan reached Delhi in July 1857 with the Bareilly brigade and was placed in charge of the rebel army, bringing some discipline to the divided camp inside the city.

 

NOTE

 

• Tantia Tope (Option 2): Tantia Tope was the principal general of Nana Sahib at Kanpur and later fought alongside Rani Laxmi Bai in Central India, not in Delhi, where the rebel army had a different commander.

 

• Khan Bahadur Khan (Option 3): Khan Bahadur Khan led the rebels at Bareilly in Rohilkhand and declared himself governor there, so he was the centre leader of a separate city, not the general in Delhi.

 

• Azimullah Khan (Option 4): Azimullah Khan was Nana Sahib's trusted lieutenant and diplomat, who had gone to England on his master's behalf, and he operated in the Kanpur centre rather than Delhi.

question: Delhi was recaptured by the British on 20 September 1857 under the leadership of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is John Nicholson.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Delhi was stormed and retaken on 20 September 1857 by British forces commanded by John Nicholson, who was mortally wounded in the fighting (20 सितंबर 1857 को जॉन निकलसन ने दिल्ली पर पुनः कब्जा किया)

 

• The fall of the Mughal capital removed the symbolic centre of the rebellion and turned the military balance toward the British.

 

• Bahadur Shah was captured and, in 1858, deported to Rangoon, where he died in 1862, while his sons were shot dead.

 

• The recapture was aided by reinforcements from Punjab, where the Sikhs had stayed loyal to the Company.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nicholson is remembered as one of the heroes of the siege, and a memorial stands at the Kashmiri Gate.

 

• Delhi's recapture is distinct from the later reconquest of Lucknow in March 1858.

 

• Bahadur Shah Zafar's burial place in Yangon is known as the Bahadur Shah Zafar Dargah.

 

• The assault on Delhi began through the Kashmiri Gate on 14 September 1857 and street fighting lasted about a week; Nicholson was wounded on the first day and died on 23 September.

 

NOTE

 

• Hugh Rose (Option 1): Sir Hugh Rose led the Central India Field Force and is associated with the storming of Jhansi in April 1858 and the capture of Gwalior, not with the recapture of Delhi.

 

• Colin Campbell (Option 2): Sir Colin Campbell was the Commander-in-Chief who relieved Lucknow in 1857 and retook the city in 1858; his campaign concerned Awadh rather than the fall of Delhi.

 

• Henry Havelock (Option 4): Henry Havelock advanced to retake Kanpur and tried to relieve the Lucknow Residency in 1857, and he died of dysentery in Lucknow in November 1857, so he did not take Delhi.

question: After the suppression of the Revolt, Bahadur Shah Zafar was:
option_1: restored to the Delhi throne as a titular ruler
option_2: hanged at Delhi along with his sons
option_3: exiled to Andaman where he died in 1870
option_4: deported to Rangoon, where he died in 1862
solution_text:
The correct answer is deported to Rangoon, where he died in 1862.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The last Mughal emperor was captured after Delhi fell, tried by the British, and deported to Rangoon (Burma) in 1858, where he died in 1862 (बहादुर शाह ज़फ़र को रंगून निर्वासित किया गया)

 

• His sons were shot dead by the British after the capture, which ended the Mughal line's claim to Delhi.

 

• The Mughal dynasty thus formally ended, and direct Crown rule over India followed with the Government of India Act of 1858.

 

• He was not executed, because the British preferred exile to avoid making a martyr of the elderly emperor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bahadur Shah Zafar wrote Urdu ghazals, and one of his famous couplets laments having no land in which to be buried.

 

• He was kept in a modest house in Rangoon and buried there; his dargah is now a memorial site.

 

• Hodson had persuaded him to surrender at Humayun's Tomb on a promise that his life would be spared.

 

NOTE

 

• restored to the Delhi throne as a titular ruler (Option 1): He was not restored to the throne; the British ended the Mughal line altogether and Delhi came under direct administration, with the emperor treated as a state prisoner and rebel.

 

• hanged at Delhi along with his sons (Option 2): He was not hanged; the British promised to spare his life when Hodson took him at Humayun's Tomb, though his sons were shot, so the claim of execution with his sons is false.

 

• exiled to Andaman where he died in 1870 (Option 3): He was sent to Rangoon in Burma, not the Andamans, and died in 1862, not 1870, so this option gets both the place of exile and the year of death wrong.

question: Nana Sahib, who led the revolt at Kanpur, was the adopted son of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Baji Rao II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nana Sahib (Dhondu Pant) was the adopted son of Baji Rao II, the last Peshwa, who lived at Bithur near Kanpur on a Company pension (नाना साहब, अंतिम पेशवा बाजीराव द्वितीय के दत्तक पुत्र)

 

• When Baji Rao II died in 1851, Dalhousie refused to continue the pension of eight lakh rupees and the title of Peshwa to the adopted heir.

 

• This refusal made Nana Sahib a bitter enemy and he joined the rebels in 1857, with Tantia Tope and Azimullah Khan as his supporters.

 

• He took Kanpur and expelled the British garrison, but British forces later recaptured the city.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nana Sahib's fate after 1858 remains uncertain, and he is believed to have escaped to Nepal.

 

• The refusal of the pension was linked to Dalhousie's rule that adopted sons did not inherit titles.

 

• Baji Rao II had lost his throne to the British after the Third Anglo-Maraṭha War of 1817-18.

 

NOTE

 

• Baji Rao I (Option 1): Baji Rao I (1720-40) was a great Peshwa who expanded Maratha power in the north; he lived about a century before Nana Sahib and was not his adoptive father.

 

• Balaji Baji Rao (Option 2): Balaji Baji Rao, the Peshwa defeated at Panipat in 1761, belongs to the eighteenth century and has no adoptive link with Nana Sahib of the 1857 Revolt.

 

• Madhav Rao II (Option 4): Madhav Rao II was a young Peshwa who died in 1795 and could not have adopted a man who rose in 1857; Nana Sahib's adoptive father was the last Peshwa.

question: Tantia Tope served as the principal general of which leader during the Revolt of 1857?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nana Sahib.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tantia Tope (Ramchandra Pandurang) was the chief military commander of Nana Sahib at Kanpur, and led the rebel forces there (तात्या टोपे नाना साहब के सेनापति थे)

 

• After Kanpur was lost he joined Rani Laxmi Bai, and together they captured Gwalior in 1858.

 

• Hugh Rose later defeated him; he was betrayed, captured and hanged by the British in April 1859.

 

• His guerrilla-style marches across central India kept the British engaged long after the northern cities had fallen.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tantia Tope had earlier been an associate of Baji Rao II's household at Bithur.

 

• He was betrayed by Raja Man Singh of Narwar, according to standard accounts, and was tried at Shivpuri.

 

• Azimullah Khan was another close associate of Nana Sahib.

 

• After Kanpur was retaken, Tantia Tope moved his forces to Kalpi and then Gwalior, using fast marches and surprise attacks that made him one of the most elusive rebel commanders.

 

NOTE

 

• Bahadur Shah Zafar (Option 2): Bahadur Shah Zafar's army was commanded by Bakht Khan at Delhi; Tantia Tope never served as the Mughal emperor's general, but was attached to the Peshwa's adopted son.

 

• Begum Hazrat Mahal (Option 3): Begum Hazrat Mahal led the rising at Lucknow with her own officers and her minor son Birjis Qadr, and she did not rely on Tantia Tope as her chief general.

 

• Kunwar Singh (Option 4): Kunwar Singh was an aged zamindar of Jagdishpur who led the revolt in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh through his own forces, not as a subordinate of Tantia Tope.

question: Which of the following was a leader of the revolt at Lucknow?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Begum Hazrat Mahal.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Begum Hazrat Mahal, wife of the deposed Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, led the rising at Lucknow in Awadh and proclaimed her son Birjis Qadr as Nawab (बेगम हज़रत महल लखनऊ में विद्रोह की नेता थीं)

 

• Awadh had been annexed in 1856 on the charge of misgovernance, and the sudden loss of the kingdom angered the taluqdars and sepoys of the region.

 

• The Residency at Lucknow was besieged by the rebels for many months until Colin Campbell's forces relieved it.

 

• After the British retook Lucknow in 1858, the Begum withdrew to Nepal.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Many sepoys of the Bengal Army were recruited from Awadh, which made the annexation a personal grievance for them.

 

• Henry Lawrence, the Chief Commissioner of Awadh, was killed during the siege of the Residency.

 

• A monument for the Begum stands in Lucknow's Victoria Park, now renamed after her.

 

• Colin Campbell's second relief of Lucknow in November 1857 and its final recapture in March 1858 ended the main rebel resistance in Awadh, though the Begum kept up the struggle until escaping to Nepal.

 

NOTE

 

• Rani Avantibai (Option 1): Rani Avantibai Lodhi raised and led an army of about four thousand soldiers in the Mandla region of Madhya Pradesh, which lies far from Lucknow in Awadh.

 

• Rani Laxmi Bai (Option 2): Rani Laxmi Bai was the leader of the revolt at Jhansi in Bundelkhand and later at Gwalior, and she did not lead the rising in Awadh's capital.

 

• Bakht Khan (Option 4): Bakht Khan commanded the rebel army in Delhi for the Mughal emperor, so he is linked with the Delhi centre rather than the Awadh centre of Lucknow.

question: Who stormed Jhansi in April 1858 and later captured Gwalior from the rebels?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sir Hugh Rose.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sir Hugh Rose, commanding the Central India Field Force, stormed Jhansi in April 1858 and then defeated Tantia Tope and recaptured Gwalior (ह्यू रोज़ ने झाँसी पर आक्रमण किया और ग्वालियर पर कब्ज़ा किया)

 

• Rani Laxmi Bai escaped from Jhansi, joined Tantia Tope and seized Gwalior, but Rose's forces attacked there as well.

 

• The Rani died fighting as a soldier on 17 June 1858.

 

• With the fall of Gwalior, organised resistance in central India collapsed, and the Revolt is said to have effectively concluded there.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hugh Rose later became Baron Strathnairn and rose to be Commander-in-Chief in India.

 

• Jhansi was annexed by Dalhousie under the Doctrine of Lapse after Raja Gangadhar Rao's death.

 

• Scindia, the ruler of Gwalior, had stayed loyal to the British.

 

• The Central India Field Force under Rose took Jhansi on 3-4 April 1858, then defeated Tantia Tope at the Betwa and Kalpi before turning to Gwalior in June 1858.

 

NOTE

 

• Sir Colin Campbell (Option 2): Colin Campbell was the Commander-in-Chief who relieved and finally recaptured Lucknow; his operations were in Awadh, whereas Jhansi and Gwalior fell to the Central India column.

 

• John Nicholson (Option 3): John Nicholson led the assault that retook Delhi in September 1857 and died of his wounds, so he was never at Jhansi or Gwalior in 1858.

 

• Lord Canning (Option 4): Lord Canning was Governor-General and the first Viceroy, a civil administrator in Calcutta who directed the response to the Revolt but did not command troops in the field.

question: Rani Laxmi Bai was defeated and killed in the Revolt of 1857 in which period?
solution_text:
The correct answer is June 1858.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rani Laxmi Bai died fighting the British near Gwalior in June 1858 (17 June 1858), after a stirring campaign with Tantia Tope (रानी लक्ष्मीबाई जून 1858 में रणभूमि में वीरगति को प्राप्त हुईं)

 

• She had been born Manikarnika and was nicknamed Manu; her husband was Raja Gangadhar Rao of Jhansi.

 

• The Doctrine of Lapse deprived her adopted son of the throne, which is why she joined the rebels.

 

• The loss of the Rani broke the rebel resistance in central India, leaving Tantia Tope to fight on until he was captured in 1859.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Rani is remembered as a symbol of courage, and the poem 'Jhansi ki Rani' by Subhadra Kumari Chauhan popularised her story.

 

• Jhansi had fallen to Hugh Rose in April 1858, before the Gwalior campaign.

 

• Her adopted son was Damodar Rao.

 

• Her adopted son Damodar Rao was refused recognition as heir, and the Rani's reply to the British officials, 'I shall not give up my Jhansi', is widely quoted as her statement of defiance.

 

NOTE

 

• January 1861 (Option 1): January 1861 is well after the Revolt had been suppressed and the Crown had taken over; by that date the Rani had been dead for more than two years.

 

• March 1863 (Option 2): March 1863 falls years after the suppression of the Revolt and Tantia Tope's execution; the Rani was killed in the middle of 1858, not at that late date.

 

• April 1860 (Option 4): April 1860 is also far too late, as the main fighting ended in 1858-59 and the Rani had died at Gwalior some twenty-two months before that date.

question:
Consider the following statements about Rani Laxmi Bai:

1. Her husband was Raja Gangadhar Rao of Jhansi.

2. The child adopted by the couple in 1853 was not recognised as heir because of the Doctrine of Lapse.

3. She was captured alive by Hugh Rose and hanged at Jhansi.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Gangadhar Rao was the Raja of Jhansi, and the Rani, nicknamed Manu, was his wife (रानी लक्ष्मीबाई के पति राजा गंगाधर राव थे)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: after the couple adopted a son in 1853, the Company applied the Doctrine of Lapse introduced by Dalhousie, refused to recognise him and annexed Jhansi.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: she was never captured or hanged, because she died a soldier's death on the battlefield on 17 June 1858 while fighting near Gwalior.

 

• It was Tantia Tope, not the Rani, who was captured and hanged by the British.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jhansi was lost to Hugh Rose in April 1858, after which the Rani joined Tantia Tope.

 

• The Doctrine of Lapse annexed Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1849), Jhansi (1853) and Nagpur (1854).

 

• The Rani's adopted son Damodar Rao later lived under British pensions.

 

• Gangadhar Rao died in November 1853 after adopting Damodar Rao, and Dalhousie's government annexed Jhansi in 1854, which pushed the Rani into the camp of the rebels in 1857.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): This pairing leaves out the first statement, which is true, since Raja Gangadhar Rao was indeed the Rani's husband; it also wrongly counts the false claim of her hanging as correct.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Statement 2 on the Doctrine of Lapse and the unrecognised adopted child is true, so leaving it out is a mistake; statement 3 about capture and hanging is false, so this combination has two defects.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Including all three would mean accepting that she was hanged, but she died in battle at Gwalior in June 1858; the third statement is false and spoils this choice.

question: Kunwar Singh, the aged leader of the Revolt of 1857, was the chief organiser of the rising in:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bihar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kunwar Singh of Jagdishpur (near Arrah) was the chief organiser of the revolt in Bihar, and he led it even though he was around eighty years old (कुँवर सिंह बिहार में विद्रोह के प्रमुख संगठनकर्ता थे)

 

• He mobilised sepoys of the Danapur garrison and local peasants, fought pitched battles and captured Arrah.

 

• He also marched into Uttar Pradesh, to Azamgarh and Lucknow, harassing British forces with guerrilla methods.

 

• He died in April 1858 soon after recapturing Jagdishpur from the British, and his brother Amar Singh continued the struggle.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kunwar Singh was a Rajput zamindar who had been heavily in debt to the Company before 1857.

 

• Peer Ali Khan was another leader of the revolt in the Patna region of Bihar.

 

• Patna was a centre where British officials arrested leaders and hanged them.

 

• Kunwar Singh fought battles at Arrah, Azamgarh and Jagdishpur, and legend records that he was wounded in the arm while crossing the Ganges and cut it off himself before reaching home.

 

NOTE

 

• Punjab (Option 1): Punjab remained largely loyal to the British during 1857 because Sikh soldiers helped to recapture Delhi, and no major rebel force there was led by Kunwar Singh.

 

• Rajasthan (Option 2): Rajasthan saw only scattered mutinies, such as at Nasirabad and Neemuch, and Kunwar Singh, who belonged to Jagdishpur, did not organise the revolt in this region.

 

• Gujarat (Option 4): Gujarat was far from Kunwar Singh's base; the main leaders were in the north and centre, and his activity centred on Bihar, Azamgarh and Awadh, not western India.

question: Peer Ali Khan organised the rebels and challenged British rule in which major city of Bihar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Patna.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Peer Ali Khan, a bookseller by occupation, organised the rebels at Patna and challenged British rule in Bihar (पीर अली खान ने पटना में विद्रोहियों को संगठित किया)

 

• He was arrested by the British authorities in Patna, and was hanged in July 1857 for his role in the uprising.

 

• He worked alongside Kunwar Singh, who was the chief organiser of the revolt in the Bihar region.

 

• His execution shows that civilian townsmen, not only sepoys, took part in the Revolt.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Patna Commissioner William Tayler dealt harshly with the Patna rebels.

 

• Bihar saw a rising at Danapur cantonment in July 1857, which helped to spread the revolt.

 

• Peer Ali is remembered with a memorial at Patna in Bihar.

 

• The Danapur sepoys rose in July 1857, joined Kunwar Singh at Arrah, and the Patna authorities responded by arresting Peer Ali and several associates, many of whom were hanged.

 

NOTE

 

• Gaya (Option 2): Gaya in south Bihar was not the city where Peer Ali Khan rallied the rebels; his movement is associated with Patna, the capital of the province and a bigger centre of the insurgents.

 

• Bhagalpur (Option 3): Bhagalpur in eastern Bihar saw only minor disturbances, and the rebel organisation of Peer Ali Khan was tied to Patna and not to this city.

 

• Muzaffarpur (Option 4): Muzaffarpur in north Bihar was a quieter district during the revolt, with no major role for Peer Ali Khan, who is known as the Patna rebel leader.

question: Khan Bahadur Khan was the leader of the Revolt of 1857 at:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bareilly.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Khan Bahadur Khan, a descendant of the Rohilla chief Hafiz Rahmat Khan, led the rebels at Bareilly in Rohilkhand (खान बहादुर खान बरेली के विद्रोही नेता थे)

 

• He set up a rebel administration in Bareilly in 1857 and defied the British for about a year.

 

• After the British under Colin Campbell recaptured Bareilly in 1858, he was captured and hanged.

 

• Bareilly is one of the centres listed with its leader, together with Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Bihar and Faizabad.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bakht Khan, the Delhi commander, also came from Bareilly with his troops.

 

• Rohilkhand had earlier lost its autonomy through the Rohilla War of the 1770s.

 

• Bareilly lies in present-day Uttar Pradesh.

 

• Hafiz Rahmat Khan, Khan Bahadur's ancestor, had been the Rohilla chief killed at Miranpur Katra in 1774 by Awadh and Company forces, giving the family a long memory of British interference.

 

NOTE

 

• Faizabad (Option 1): Faizabad was the area where Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah led the rising, so this centre has a different leader and is not associated with Khan Bahadur Khan.

 

• Mandla (Option 2): Mandla in Madhya Pradesh was where Rani Avantibai Lodhi organised an army of four thousand soldiers; it is not linked with Khan Bahadur Khan of Rohilkhand.

 

• Kanpur (Option 4): Kanpur was led by Nana Sahib with Tantia Tope and Azimullah as his supporters, which makes it a separate centre from the Rohilkhand stronghold of Khan Bahadur.

question: Rani Avantibai Lodhi is remembered in the Revolt of 1857 for leading an army of about four thousand soldiers in the region of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mandla.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rani Avantibai Lodhi of Ramgarh raised and led an army of nearly four thousand soldiers against the East India Company in the Mandla region of Madhya Pradesh (रानी अवंतीबाई लोधी ने मंडला क्षेत्र में विद्रोह का नेतृत्व किया)

 

• She became the ruler's regent after her husband's death, and the Company tried to take over the estate, which pushed her into rebellion.

 

• She fought courageously and, when surrounded, chose to take her own life rather than surrender in 1858.

 

• She represents the participation of women and tribal chiefs of central India in the Revolt.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mandla is in the Gondwana region and the Narmada valley.

 

• Many local Gond and Lodhi chiefs joined her in the fight.

 

• A memorial stamp has honoured her.

 

• Her husband's death left the Ramgarh state under a minor heir, and the Company's Court of Wards took charge of the estate, a step that angered her and led her to take up arms.

 

NOTE

 

• Jhansi (Option 1): Jhansi was the seat of Rani Laxmi Bai, a different queen who fought the British in Bundelkhand and later at Gwalior; Avantibai's army operated elsewhere.

 

• Faizabad (Option 2): Faizabad is in Awadh and was the area of Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah, so it does not match the region where Rani Avantibai raised her army of four thousand.

 

• Arrah (Option 3): Arrah in Bihar was the area of Kunwar Singh's operations, and it lies far from the central Indian region of Mandla where Avantibai fought.

question:
Match the leader with the centre of the Revolt of 1857:

Leader: (a) Nana Sahib (b) Begum Hazrat Mahal (c) Maulavi Ahmadullah (d) Khan Bahadur Khan

Centre: (i) Faizabad (ii) Bareilly (iii) Kanpur (iv) Lucknow
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nana Sahib led the rebels at Kanpur, supported by Tantia Tope and Azimullah, so (a) matches (iii) (नाना साहब - कानपुर; हज़रत महल - लखनऊ)

 

• Begum Hazrat Mahal of Awadh directed the rising at Lucknow, so (b) matches (iv).

 

• Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah was the leader at Faizabad in Awadh, so (c) matches (i); he was a popular preacher who raised the banner there.

 

• Khan Bahadur Khan controlled Bareilly in Rohilkhand, so (d) matches (ii).

 

• Delhi, Jhansi, Bihar and Mandla complete the list of principal centres: Bahadur Shah II and Bakht Khan, Rani Laxmi Bai, Kunwar Singh, and Rani Avantibai Lodhi respectively.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kanpur, Lucknow, Faizabad and Bareilly all lie in the Awadh and Rohilkhand belt of present-day Uttar Pradesh.

 

• Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah was killed in 1858 by the Raja of Powayan, who betrayed him.

 

• Delhi, Jhansi, Bihar and Mandla were the other centres with Bakht Khan, Laxmi Bai, Kunwar Singh and Avantibai respectively.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii (Option 1): This version swaps Nana Sahib and Begum Hazrat Mahal, giving Nana Sahib to Lucknow and the Begum to Kanpur, although Nana Sahib's seat was Kanpur and Hazrat Mahal's was Lucknow.

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i (Option 3): Here Maulavi Ahmadullah is linked with Bareilly and Khan Bahadur Khan with Faizabad, which is the reverse of the true pairing, since Bareilly was Khan Bahadur's base.

 

• a-i, b-iv, c-iii, d-ii (Option 4): Nana Sahib is put at Faizabad and Maulavi Ahmadullah at Kanpur, which is wrong, because Nana Sahib was the Kanpur leader and the Maulavi was the Faizabad leader.

question: The policy of annexation known as the 'Doctrine of Lapse', one of the political causes of the Revolt of 1857, was introduced by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Dalhousie.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Doctrine of Lapse was introduced by Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General 1848-56): states whose rulers died without a natural male heir were annexed (डलहौजी की हड़प नीति)

 

• Under it Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1849), Jhansi (1853) and Nagpur (1854) were absorbed into British territory.

 

• The adopted heirs of Indian rulers were refused recognition, and titles and pensions such as Nana Sahib's were ended.

 

• These annexations made the old ruling houses fear for their survival and made them join the Revolt, which makes the doctrine a major political cause.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The doctrine was abolished after the Revolt, and the Queen's Proclamation of 1858 recognised the right of adoption.

 

• Dalhousie also annexed Awadh in 1856 on the charge of misgovernance, not under Lapse.

 

• Wellesley's own tool of expansion was the Subsidiary Alliance.

 

• Among states taken by lapse were Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853) and Nagpur (1854), apart from Awadh, annexed for misrule.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Wellesley (Option 1): Lord Wellesley (1798-1805) used the Subsidiary Alliance to bring Indian states under control; this was an earlier system and not the Doctrine of Lapse of the 1850s.

 

• Lord Canning (Option 2): Lord Canning was Governor-General when the Revolt broke out and he ended the doctrine in the aftermath; he did not introduce it.

 

• Lord Cornwallis (Option 4): Lord Cornwallis (1786-93) is known for the Permanent Settlement and judicial reforms, and he had nothing to do with annexation by lapse, which is a Dalhousie measure.

question: Awadh was annexed by the British in 1856 on the charge of misgovernance. Which Nawab was deposed in this annexation?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Wajid Ali Shah.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Wajid Ali Shah, the last Nawab of Awadh, was removed in 1856 on the charge of misgovernance and was sent to Calcutta (वाजिद अली शाह को 1856 में अवध से हटाया गया)

 

• Lord Dalhousie carried out the annexation, but not under the Doctrine of Lapse, since the Nawab had a legitimate heir.

 

• The annexation hurt the many sepoys of the Bengal Army recruited from Awadh, and the taluqdars lost their estates.

 

• Begum Hazrat Mahal, Wajid Ali Shah's wife, led the resistance at Lucknow in 1857.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Wajid Ali Shah was a patron of music and the Kathak dance and a poet.

 

• Awadh was the heartland from which the Company recruited its high-caste sepoys.

 

• Dalhousie had called Awadh a cherry that would drop into the mouth of the Company.

 

• Wajid Ali Shah was sent to Matiabruz near Calcutta with a pension, and the annexation was supported by the Resident Outram's report on the misgovernment of the kingdom.

 

NOTE

 

• Saadat Ali Khan (Option 1): Saadat Ali Khan was the Nawab of Awadh from 1798 to 1814 and accepted a Subsidiary-style treaty with the Company, so he lived decades before the annexation of 1856.

 

• Asaf-ud-Daula (Option 3): Asaf-ud-Daula ruled Awadh from 1775 to 1797 and shifted the capital to Lucknow; he died long before the annexation and cannot be the Nawab deposed in 1856.

 

• Shuja-ud-Daula (Option 4): Shuja-ud-Daula was defeated at the Battle of Buxar in 1764 and died in 1775, so he belongs to the age of Plassey and Buxar rather than to the Revolt.

question:
Consider the following statements about the grievance of Nana Sahib:

1. He was the adopted son of Baji Rao II.

2. The Company refused to continue the pension of Baji Rao II to him.

3. He was granted the title of Peshwa by Lord Canning in 1856.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Nana Sahib was the adopted son of the last Peshwa Baji Rao II and lived at Bithur (नाना साहब बाजीराव द्वितीय के दत्तक पुत्र थे)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: after Baji Rao II died in 1851 Dalhousie refused to extend the pension to the adopted son, treating it as a personal grant and not an inheritance.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: no title of Peshwa was ever conferred on him by the Company, and the refusal of recognition was one of the political grievances behind his role in 1857.

 

• He then joined the rebels at Kanpur, with Tantia Tope and Azimullah as his lieutenants.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Baji Rao II had surrendered to John Malcolm in 1818 and was given a pension of eight lakh rupees and the estate at Bithur.

 

• The refusal of Nana Sahib's pension belongs among the political causes of the Revolt along with the annexation of Awadh and Jhansi.

 

• Azimullah Khan had gone to London to plead Nana Sahib's case.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 only (Option 1): Statement 2 is also true, since the pension was indeed refused; limiting the answer to the first statement ignores the pension grievance that pushed Nana Sahib toward rebellion.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Statement 3 is false, because the Company never gave Nana Sahib the Peshwa's title, and this combination also fails to include the first statement, which is correct.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Statement 3 is false, as Canning never gave Nana Sahib the title of Peshwa; accepting all three statements therefore wrongly turns a refusal into a grant.

question: The Widow Remarriage Act, 1856 was passed during the Governor-Generalship of Lord Canning mainly through the efforts of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856 was drafted under Dalhousie and enacted under Canning, mainly due to the efforts of Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (विधवा पुनर्विवाह अधिनियम 1856 - ईश्वरचंद्र विद्यासागर)

 

• It legalised the remarriage of Hindu widows and gave legitimacy to their children, which struck at a long-standing social custom.

 

• Orthodox Hindus saw such laws as interference in their social life, and the notes list such legislation among the social causes of the Revolt.

 

• The earlier prohibition of Sati in 1829 by William Bentinck was achieved with the efforts of Raja Ram Mohan Roy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vidyasagar's Bengali petition in 1855 collected nearly a thousand signatures for the act.

 

• The first widow remarriage under the act was performed in Calcutta in December 1856.

 

• Vidyasagar was also a pioneer of women's education and Principal of Sanskrit College.

 

• Vidyasagar relied on Hindu scriptures, quoting the Parashara Smriti, to argue that widow remarriage was permissible, and he supported the first marriages from his own funds.

 

NOTE

 

• Raja Ram Mohan Roy (Option 1): Raja Ram Mohan Roy campaigned against Sati, which Bentinck banned in 1829; he died in 1833, long before the Widow Remarriage Act of 1856, so he cannot be credited with it.

 

• Dayananda Saraswati (Option 2): Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875 and worked on reform later; he had no role in the Act of 1856, which came almost two decades earlier.

 

• Jyotiba Phule (Option 3): Jyotiba Phule worked for the education of women and lower castes in Maharashtra and founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873, which is not linked to this Act.
